entries.title: German gamblers could claim losses back
entries.summary: German gamblers may finally be able to beat the house, thanks to new court rulings in the EU and a federal court. The decisions could help gambling addicts — but the legal road might be difficult.
entries.content:
Germany

German gamblers could claim losses back

October 15, 2026

German gamblers may finally be able to beat the house, thanks to new court rulings in the EU and a federal court. The decisions could help gambling addicts — but the legal road might be difficult.

A German court has followed the European Court of Justice in finding that gamblers can seek compensation from gambling companies if they lost money when online casinos and fruit machines were illegal in Germany.

The verdicts could have major consequences for gambling addicts, as thousands of people could potentially bring civil lawsuits against gambling companies.

A series of court decisions at regional, federal, and European level have found in favor of gamblers in the last year, beginning with the Higher Regional Court Stuttgart in September 2025, which agreed with a plaintiff in the state of Baden-Württemberg who sued the Malta-based online betting company Tipico Games.

The plaintiff lost around €10,000 ($11,200) between 2020 and 2022, but because online gambling was prohibited in Germany until 2021, the court found that operators had therefore received the winnings without legal basis and must return them.

Wins for the losers

Tipico Games then appealed to the Federal Court of Justice (BGH), the highest civil and criminal court in Germany. In an initial verbal hearing in mid-September this year, the court followed the principle of the plaintiffs' case on one key point: That gamblers have the right to claim back losses if the companies did not have a license in Germany at the time the losses were incurred. But a final decision on the case is only expected to be made in January next year.

Online casinos and fruit machines were banned in Germany from 2008 to 2021, but several gambling operators were active in the country because they had gaming licenses in other EU countries.

In April this year, the European Court of Justice ruled that EU law does not preclude a member state from "prohibiting certain services," or from "attaching civil-law consequences to that prohibition." In other words, even if a gambling company has a legitimate license in one member state, that doesn't override national gambling laws elsewhere.

Thomas Dünchheim, a business lawyer at global law firm Greenberg Traurig who specializes in gambling law, said law firms were now gathering clients — sometimes trawling the internet with the help of AI tools — to prepare massive collective lawsuits. Dünchheim himself has people who have lost tens of thousands of euros come to him seeking representation.

"The pendulum is swinging more and more towards the consumer. It's a bit like in America — we're seeing a mass phenomenon like the Dieselgate lawsuits against VW," he told DW. "And there are lawyers who will collect all these little cases, bundle them, and then maybe even drive it forward with the help of a legal financing firm. It's a good business for all involved, and the ones that will have to pay are the gambling firms who operated unlawful gambling in Germany."

The dangers of online gambling

The decisions could bring a measure of help for addicts, as online gambling can be particularly dangerous for people with addiction issues. According to Tobias Hayer, a psychologist at the Institute for Public Health and Nursing Research at Bremen University, that comes down to four main features of online gambling: Anonymity and the consequent lack of social control, 24/7 accessibility, the frictionless nature of cashless transactions, and the high frequency of games played.

"These court verdicts are not surprising at all," Hayer told DW, but he added that he had an ambivalent attitude to them. "On the one hand I can imagine that this will be a huge relief to many gamblers who had an addiction problem. On the other hand, if these people suddenly get a lot of money in their hands, but they haven't worked through their problems, then of course there's a danger of recidivism."

The legal obstacles

But Dünchheim suggested that the gamblers may not have such an easy ride when making their claims. It's true that German law has now concluded that if the gambling contract that the player makes with the company turns out to be unlawful in the country where they live, the player can claim their losses back. But only if the player themselves "did not act illegally," as Dünchheim put it.

"You also have to say: Many of these players deliberately went to games in this gray zone because the winnings are potentially bigger," he said. "Because the companies don't pay taxes."

"Then the defense team of the gambling company will of course say: 'You took part in an illegal game yourself, so you were acting illegally.' And this question of interpretation is not simple," he added. "It's a very interesting intellectual question, but it's also existential for the gambling companies."

Tipico's gambling gray zone

The Tipico case is perhaps particularly interesting in the German context because, although the company is based in Malta, it was founded in 2004 by a group of German lawyers. The company is a big employer, with several thousand employees worldwide, and has been a sponsor of more than one top German football club. Tipico has also said that it has rigorous consumer protection measures in place to identify and prevent dangerous betting behavior.

But there was some legal ambiguity about its online operations in Germany up until 2021. "They always had lawyers who could attest that what they are doing conforms to European law, because it is permitted in a European Union member state," said Dünchheim. "But that is a false assumption, as it has now been established that a gambling permit in another EU state doesn't apply in Germany, because unlike other areas, gambling law isn't harmonized across the bloc."

"Tipico was started by two businessmen and grew big in a gray zone," as Dünchheim put it. "They had professional lobbying firms on board and they hired experienced lawyers, they had private equity firms on board. But of course they are carrying a huge financial risk."

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

entries.title: School roof collapse in Pakistan's Peshawar kills dozens of students and one teacher
entries.summary: Local authorities said more than 50 other people were injured in the disaster. Roof collapses have become increasingly common in Pakistan.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Dozens killed in school roof collapse in Pakistan

Published October 15, 2026last updated October 15, 2026

Local authorities said more than 50 other people were injured in the disaster. Roof collapses have become increasingly common in Pakistan.

Officials in Peshawar, Pakistan, confirmed on Thursday that at least 32 pupils under the age of 13 died when an elementary school roof collapsed in the Afridi Abad area of the city.

One teacher has also died, they said. The deceased, along with more than 50 other injured people, were brought to Lady Reading Hospital as rescue workers rushed to clear the rubble and search for more survivors.

"We have taken out ​at ‌least 45 children," said district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan, but added that more children were thought to still be under the rubble.

From her hospital bed, a teacher told reporters that the school had three floors and more than 1,200 pupils and staff.

The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear.

Roof collapses becoming more regular

Local media in Pakistan noted that such incidents are becoming increasingly routine across the country, due to poor building standards and maintenance.

In July, three young girls were killed near Umerkot when the outer wall of a government school gave way. That same month, one child died and five were injured in Lahore when the roof of an under-construction private school collapsed.

One month earlier, 14 children were killed in a similar manner at a private tutoring facility in Lahore, which came shortly after yet another such incident in Dera Ghazi Khan.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as a preferred source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Germany news: Train station alcohol ban comes into force
entries.summary: Consuming alcohol is no longer permitted at train stations in Germany, to improve the lot of travelers and staff alike. Coalition talks are restarting in Berlin, and an inmate is loose in Essen. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Train station alcohol ban comes into force

Published October 15, 2026last updated October 15, 2026

Consuming alcohol is no longer permitted at train stations in Germany, to improve the lot of travelers and staff alike. Coalition talks are restarting in Berlin, and an inmate is loose in Essen. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Train stations ban alcohol consumption nationwide after trial period in dozens of towns and cities
  • Bundestag parliament approves reforms to emergency care services aiming to help paramedics and patients
  • Sharp rise in tobacco taxes set for a vote in parliament, expected to pass
  • Berlin left-leaning coalition negotiations likely to restart after major wobble earlier in the week
  • Bleak potato harvest and higher prices forecast after scorching, dry summer

Follow our roundup of headlines across Germany for Thursday, October 15.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add DW as a Preferred Source on Google

Skip next section Alcohol ban comes into force at all German train stations

Alcohol ban comes into force at all German train stations

Alcohol bans came into force at all German train stations when the clock struck midnight and Thursday began.

All the roughly 5,700 stations across Germany, including the train platforms themselves, are now booze-free zones. 

Pubs, restaurants and other such hospitality businesses at train stations are exceptions to the rule, though, and can still serve alcohol. Consumption of alcohol will also remain legal on many trains, with long distance ones still serving beers and other tipples at their on-board bistros.

Rail operator Deutsche Bahn says the change aims to make train stations safer and cleaner, and more pleasant places to spend time waiting for a (who knows, perhaps delayed) train. 

Various misdemeanors and incidents had prompted discussions on alcohol at stations over the years, but two this year in particular brought the issues into sharp focus.

A 26-year-old security staff member for Deutsche Bahn was beaten and kicked by a drunken passenger when trying to check their ticket. During the struggle the train door buckled and opened, and the Bahn employee fell from the train, suffering severe injuries. Earlier in the year, a train conductor was killed when attacked by a man without a valid ticket.

The new rules are part of DB's house rules, rather than being criminal law — meaning that at least in the first instance it is a matter for Bahn security staff to enforce rather than police.

"The alcohol consumption ban applies at stations every day, also on days with major events," Bahn spokeswoman Anja Bröder said when asked about often beer-fueled train usage days, like when football fans flock to Bundesliga games.

Around 40 stations piloted the project for some time prior to its implementation, including some of the largest like Cologne, Munich, Hamburg and Berlin. DB says it has had positive experiences with the early experiments, reporting more peaceful stations with less litter and travelers and employees saying they preferred the atmosphere.

A federal group dedicated to helping the homeless has criticized the measure, however, saying that for homeless people with addiction illnesses, train stations often served as "important, weatherproof and comparatively safe places" to shelter. A spokeswoman also told the Rheinische Post newspaper that if they were driven from sites like train stations, it would be harder for social workers to locate them.

Skip next section Welcome to our updates

Welcome to our updates

Alla hopp! Another day, another digest of the main news morsels on the menu in fair Deutschland, delectable and perhaps disgusting alike. Thanks for stopping by, Planet Earth.

If you're waiting for a train and frustrated by the delay — hardly an unthinkable scenario in modern Germany — on no account crack open a beer to wile away the time. Starting this Thursday, booze is banned at all of the country's train stations. It's part of a bid to improve behavior, fight littering and in extreme cases protect travelers and staff alike.

Various reform plans should start the parliamentary reading process in the Bundestag, after the Cabinet signed off on them in a Wednesday meeting. These include hikes to tobacco taxes, emergency service reforms, and changes to the federal law on support in education.

The Bundestag will also vote, in what's probably a formality, on extending the military peacekeeping deployments in the Red Sea and in South Sudan into 2027.

Left-leaning coalition negotiations are set to restart in Berlin after hitting a big bump in the road earlier this week.

Essen police are still searching for a prisoner who was violently freed from custody yesterday by two accomplices during a doctor's visit.

And the government stats office is warning of a meager potato harvest and increased prices after the scorching, dry summer.

We'll endeavor to keep you abreast of these stories and whatever else breaks as the day develops.

entries.title: Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why
entries.summary: Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.
entries.content:
October 15, 2026

Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

Few national elections carry as much environmental weight as Brazil's presidential race. And this one is being watched from far beyond the country's boundaries.

Home to the largest section of the Amazon rainforest, Brazil is guardian of a carbon sink of vital importance, making the country's conservation policies globally relevant. 

Environmentalists have already voiced alarm at Flávio Bolsonaro — son of right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro — coming out 2% ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of elections.

"It's going to be a second coming of Bolsonaro, therefore a more radical Bolsonaro," said Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian NGOs.

"At the risk of sounding alarmist, I would say Lula's re-election is the only thing standing between us and the end of the Amazon."

Amazon rainforest: One of nature's most powerful defenses

The Amazon rainforest stores huge amounts of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere from the burning of fossil fuels. As a result, it helps regulate the Earth's climate.

For decades, the tropical forest has acted as one of nature's most powerful defenses against climate change. But it has also suffered from widespread deforestation. 

During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, from 2019 until 2023, environmental agencies were weakened and enforcement efforts curtailed, meaning tropical forest was cleared at unprecedented rates.

"The environment agenda was disregarded and the level of control the government had on pollution overall, but specifically on deforestation, was reversed," said Claudio Forner, head of climate policy at Berlin-based think tank Climate Analytics.

Over Bolsonaro's four-year term, an estimated 45,586km2 of the Amazon was destroyed, an area bigger than the size of Denmark. And the forest is not as resilient as it once was, with scientists warning that parts of it are now emitting more carbon than they absorb.

Lula came to office with a message of protection for the Amazon. Besides calling for an end to deforestation by 2030, he increased monitoring of the forest and strengthened Brazil's environmental enforcement agency IBAMA.

Deforestation has plummeted under his leadership, with 2026 set to be its lowest level in a decade. That represents a 41% drop overall compared to Jair Bolsonaro's tenure.

Pitting environment against the economy

Experts have already criticized Flávio Bolsonaro's record on forest protection. As a senator in 2019, he authored draft legislation that could have stark impacts for the Amazon. While landowners are currently required to preserve 80% of their property for the growth of native plants, the bill would allow them to use their holdings as they please.

"The signal from the president will say 'now you can deforest' or 'it's harder to deforest,'" said Ana Yang, director of the Environment and Society Center at London-based think tank Chatham House.

"The moment that you decrease enforcement capability, deforestation grows," she told DW.

Bolsonaro has also pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year before Lula. But Claudio Angelo is critical of that message.

"He will end illegal deforestation not by enforcing the law, but by making it legal," he said.

More generally, environmental experts fear Bolsonaro might dismantle many of the protections strengthened under the current president.

"Unfortunately, climate change has become a partisan issue, so rather than offering a solution from their perspective, the right pictures climate change as an invented problem...that regulation goes against economic growth or it goes against competitiveness, that it's the aim of the left to control the means of production," Forner said.

In an interview with Brazilian media in August, Bolsonaro said he regarded extreme weather events to be cyclical and did not believe they were solely linked to human influence.

No straightforward climate success story for Brazil

A Bolsonaro win is likely to see Brazil move away from its position as a climate leader, a role the country embraced last year as it hosted the COP30 climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belem.

But even a Lula victory would not represent a straightforward climate success story, say experts. While the current administration has overseen significant reductions in deforestation, it has also backed plans to expand oil production.

Angelo said the decision to allow exploratory drilling was a "betrayal" of Lula's mandate but added that the president's overall record on climate had been "quite impressive".

"Lula is the world's worst climate leader, except for all the others," he told DW.

The current president will face a runoff election with Bolsonaro on October 25. But while experts say the outcome could determine the fate of the Amazon and the wider efforts to curb global warming, for many Brazilians climate is not high on their list of priorities.

"Ultimately what people care about is access to education, sanitation and health," said Yang. A road built through the Amazon to access those services, while criticized from outside Brazil for destroying parts of the rainforest, would be desirable to voters, she added.

"They don't have time to care. Not because they don't want to. They care about their own survival," she said.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: India news: Supreme Court hears Rahul Gandhi's Election Commission plea
entries.summary: A petition filed by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and others seeks an independent audit of India's sweeping voter deletions. Meanwhile, actor Imran Khan has reportedly been ordered to leave India. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India: Top court hears Rahul Gandhi's Election Commission plea

Published October 15, 2026last updated October 15, 2026

A petition filed by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and others seeks an independent audit of India's sweeping voter deletions. Meanwhile, actor Imran Khan has reportedly been ordered to leave India. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here are the latest developments from India on Thursday, October 15:

  • Supreme Court is hearing Rahul Gandhi-led petition against revision of voter lists
  • Actor Imran Khan ordered to leave India over participation in protests, reports say
  • Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar meets UAE counterpart Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan
  • Three Indian nationals killed in Germany building fire, arson suspected

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Rahul Gandhi's key petition on mass voter deletions listed in Supreme Court today

Rahul Gandhi's key petition on mass voter deletions listed in Supreme Court today

The Supreme Court is slated to hear a petition filed by India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and several other opposition lawmakers over a sweeping exercise which has so far purged over 130 million names from the country's electoral rolls.

A list of cases to be taken up on Thursday by a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant shows the petition named "Rahul Gandhi and others versus Election Commission of India and others."

The plea was filed on Monday at the end of a protest march to the Supreme Court that saw Congress' Gandhi rallying thousands, including members of the opposition INDIA bloc, student leaders, activists and civil society, through a heavily barricaded part of the capital. 

The protest was the latest in a series of demonstrations calling for India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The poll body, whose neutrality has come under scrutiny, rejects the allegations and says the exercise, called Special Intensive Revision (SIR), removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Modi's party has also dismissed the accusations and deems the protests as attempts to "create anarchy."

Meanwhile, neither Modi nor Kumar have publicly addressed the issue.

Gandhi's petition seeks an interim suspension of the nationwide revision of voter rolls, along with an audit of voter deletions and safeguards against deletions without prior notice.

Skip next section India expected to overtake Japan as 4th largest economy in 2027 — IMF

India expected to overtake Japan as 4th largest economy in 2027 — IMF

India is expected to overtake Japan to become the fourth-largest economy in the world by next year, according to projections released by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Thursday.

The Washington-based organization said that while this year Japan would continue to hold its spot as the fourth-largest nation by nominal gross domestic product, India was set to take over with a GDP estimated at $4.52 trillion (€4.03 trillion) in 2027.

The projection showed Japan sliding to sixth place next year, ranking behind India and the United Kingdom.

The United States leads as the world's largest economy, followed by China and Germany.

The IMF's Asia and Pacific Department Director Krishna Srinivasan said India entered the ongoing energy price shock caused by the Middle East conflict from a strong position.

"Growth was strong, fiscal prudence was pretty much enshrined, they had lots of reserves and so on," he said. "And so in that context, they have responded well to the shock."

Skip next section Supreme Court seeks response from Election Commission to Rahul Gandhi's plea

Supreme Court seeks response from Election Commission to Rahul Gandhi's plea

The Supreme Court has issued a notice to the Election Commission of India and the body's three commissioners, including top official Gyanesh Kumar, seeking their response over a petition filed by Congress' Rahul Gandhi.

The opposition leader and other lawmakers had filed the petition over alleged irregularities in a widespread revision of the country's electoral rolls.

The court said it would group the petition together with several pending pleas related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists.

"We are issuing notice and tagging it with the matters already pending. Somebody will accept notice on behalf of the Election Commission of India. Otherwise, serve them," legal news website Bar and Bench cited the top court as saying.

Gandhi and leaders of the INDIA bloc of opposition parties filed the plea on October 12, following a massive protest march to the Supreme Court.

The protest was among a flurry of demonstrations that the nation has witnessed in recent weeks, calling for Kumar's resignation.

It came after a newspaper investigation found Kumar allegedly took unilateral decisions that resulted in a mass deletion of voters, allegedly violating the law.

The Indian Express reported that two of Kumar's fellow election commissioners raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral roll data but those concerns were not taken into consideration.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court also issued a notice in another plea to Gandhi, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav and other protesters over their Monday march to its complex.

The march came after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant turned down a request by the opposition for a meeting to submit a memorandum on issues related to the SIR, saying that discussing issues already pending before the court would go against the principle of separation of powers.

Skip next section READ — India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping

READ — India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping

India has urged both Russia and Ukraine to ensure safe passage for commercial shipping through the Black Sea as attacks on merchant vessels put Indian seafarers at risk and threaten to disrupt vital food and energy supplies. 

New Delhi says discussions with both sides are under way.

India accounts for more than 12% of the global seafaring workforce, with 311,936 maritime professionals, according to a 2026 industry report. And attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Black Sea in recent months have highlighted the risks facing civilian crews.

Click here for a detailed report.

Skip next section Actor Imran Khan asked to leave India over anti-election chief protest

Actor Imran Khan asked to leave India over anti-election chief protest

Bollywood actor Imran Khan has been issued a notice by the Mumbai Police, asking him to leave the country over his participation in a protest against India's top poll official last week, reports said Thursday.

Khan, who is a US national, was briefly detained during the protest against alleged voter roll manipulation held at August Kranti Maidan in Maharashtra's Mumbai city on Saturday.

Khan had posted a picture of himself on Instagram from inside a police van.

"Apparently I'm going for a drive," he said in the post.

Videos of him being pulled inside the van by police officials subsequently went viral on social media.

The notice directs Khan to leave India by October 28 for allegedly violating provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, reports said.

The vice president of Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) Maharashtra unit, Kirit Somaiya, had earlier called for Khan to be arrested and deported over alleged violations of Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) provisions and visa norms.

Speaking to the media before he was detained on Saturday, Khan said that he had come to the protest location as a citizen of Mumbai and was not there with any specific demands.

"I don't have demands. I am here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I am here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted. Why are people's voices being suppressed? That is why I am here," he said.

Khan is the nephew of prominent Bollywood actor Aamir Khan.

Skip next section Three Indians killed in Germany building fire, arson suspected

Three Indians killed in Germany building fire, arson suspected

Three Indian nationals were killed in a fire at an apartment building in western Germany's Bochum. 

The Indian Embassy in Berlin said in a statement that two women and one man were among those who died, adding that all three were studying in Germany.

According to German media reports, the victims were aged between 25 and 27. Five other people were injured.

German news agency DPA said that the fire department received an alert at 4:15 a.m. local time (0212 GMT/UTC). Residents were seen calling for help as they stood at windows on the first and second floors of the building, DPA reported.

The firefighting efforts lasted several hours.

A technical malfunction was ruled out as the cause of the fire and authorities said they were investigating a suspected arson.

A 41-year-old man, who is a resident of the building, has been arrested on suspicion of murder and is in pretrial detention, reports said citing a police statement.

The reports identified the man as a Romanian national.

Meanwhile, the Indian Embassy said it was in touch with German authorities and the families of the victims. It added that it was offering all necessary assistance.

"We extend our deepest condolences to the bereaved families in this hour of grief," the statement from the embassy said.

Bochum's mayor, Jörg Lukat, called the incident a "tragedy the likes of which Bochum has not seen in decades."

Skip next section India's top diplomat in UAE for talks

India's top diplomat in UAE for talks

Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar has met United Arab Emirates' Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan while on a visit to Abu Dhabi.

Jaishankar called the meeting "warm and productive" in a post on X and said that the two sides discussed bilateral and global issues.

The Indian top diplomat's three-day visit to the UAE began on Wednesday.

A statement released by the Foreign Ministry in New Delhi earlier this week said the bilateral talks would review the progress of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership between India and the UAE.

Jaishankar is also taking part in the Raisina Middle East forum in Abu Dhabi, co-hosted by New Delhi-based think tank Observer Research Foundation and the foreign ministries of India and the UAE.

He said a discussion with Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan at the event underpinned the importance of recognizing the increasing pace of change in the global order, highlighting that it reflects "long term trends and immediate shocks."

"Countries respond as per their specific situation. New partnerships and fresh options are inevitably explored in that pursuit," he said, adding that it involved going beyond "traditional comfort zones and developing sharper strategic awareness."

Jaishankar also called for an urgent "reform of multilateralism," which he said could be supported through a more robust "minilateralism."

On Wednesday, Jaishankar also met  Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili in Abu Dhabi and discussed ways to further deepen bilateral cooperation in areas such as business, connectivity and culture. 

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our Thursday digest of all the biggest headlines that have got India talking.

The country's top court is set to hear a batch of petitions over this month's clampdown on protests called by India's 'Cockroach' movement against the election chief as ire over mass voter deletions intensifies.

The court is also expected to hear a plea filed by Congress' Rahul Gandhi and several other opposition leaders over alleged irregularities in voter lists.

On the diplomatic front, Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar is in the middle of a trip to the United Arab Emirates, where he has held talks with Deputy Prime Minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Also making news, three Indians have died in an apartment fire in the western German city of Bochum. German media reports say authorities are probing suspected arson and have arrested a building resident on suspicion of murder.

Stay with us for all this and more.

entries.title: Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums
entries.summary: From action cameras and smartphones to EVs and robot vacuums, Chinese brands are gaining ground worldwide despite privacy and security concerns. What's driving their rise, and can European rivals keep up?
entries.content:
October 15, 2026

From action cameras and smartphones to EVs and robot vacuums, Chinese brands are gaining ground worldwide despite privacy and security concerns. What's driving their rise, and can European rivals keep up?

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

The main culprit? Chinese competition.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

China's growing tech lead

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Privacy and security concerns persist

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In addition to privacy concerns, Chinese consumer tech firms have come under scrutiny over espionage and other risks, most recently regarding connected devices like EVs.

Is a new trade war brewing?

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

Can Western companies compete?

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: Manchester City, the UAE and the UK's OM in a political tangle
entries.summary: Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.
entries.content:
October 15, 2026

Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.

Defiance was the word that stood out as Manchester City returned home for the first time since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges by the Premier League in a case that's made headlines around the world.

City showed a measure of it on the pitch, even as they lost 4-2 to holders, Qatari-owned Paris Saint-Germain, in the Champions League group stages on Wednesday.

Among the home fanbase at the Etihad Stadium, DW found universal support for City's Abu Dhabi owners — headed by Sheikh Mansour, who is also UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister.

"I'm all in with the ownership now," said local fan Matt. "If we end up back in non-league, so be it. We've got 15 years of memories we wouldn't have otherwise and to me it's just an accounting line on a spreadsheet really."

Tarnished trophies?

The stadium name itself is a reminder of the takeover that changed this club, and its part of Manchester, in 2008. The national airline of the UAE, Etihad's inflated sponsorship of City is among the key planks of the case against them, while many buildings and businesses around the stadium bear the brand. It's a stadium that's also seen plenty of success of late.

"We've seen things other fans will never see," added fellow City fan Josh. "I think people have got to consider how many people this club has given great memories to, how many people's lives have been changed by it, myself included....you've got to be grateful for that."

Though many in sky blue shared those sentiments, most outside the club now view the trophies won in the relevant period as tarnished. On top of that, critics point to City's reticence in providing evidence in their case, the long-documented human rights abuses in UAE and the often dismissive tone with which the owners have dealt with being found guilty of charges they have now appealed.

UAE links have Burnham on back foot

But those City fans appear to have one powerful ally in British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Though he has since sought to tone down his position on Mansour and co. somewhat, the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he "would be really concerned to lose them," after the verdict was announced in late September. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester," he added.

While Burnham has since denied being close to City's ownership, even as City were playing on Wednesday, The Guardian reported a club representative was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week by Burnham's successor as Manchester mayor, Bev Craig.

Earlier the same day, Burnham was forced to confirm he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality. It has become a serious domestic issue for the man who replaced Keir Starmer in July.

What is clear is that Burnham welcomed Abu Dhabi investment during his time in charge of the northwestern city. This came mainly in the form of residential and commercial buildings as well as libraries and sports centers, all popping up in previously run-down areas in and around the stadium.

UAE build where others can't

Georgina Blakeley, a Professor at the University of Huddersfield who wrote a book called "The regeneration of east Manchester," told DW that UAE investment has transformed swathes of the city.

"One of the prime drivers for building this partnership with the Abu Dhabi United Group [a private equity arm of the state mostly concerned with the football club] was that at that point in time, 2014, there was no other private investor willing to invest at the scale that the council wanted. And to do so in a way that created a build-to-rent market," she said.

The UAE investment in Manchester, accelerated by the Manchester Life Partnership with the city's council signed in 2014, has been a key defense for the City owners and fans when faced with sportswashing allegations in the past. And while Blakeley believes councils in the UK are often forced to seek foreign investment, there has been some pushback on how east Manchester has changed.

"A lot of people would be critical of some of the developments in [the districts of] Ancoats and New Islington and say that it's gentrified the area and there are some tensions between newer populations coming in and living in the more expensive flats and those already there. I think there's some truth to it. But I also think there's some truth to the fact that people forget really, really quickly that if you go back to just the 1990s, Ancoats was a no-go area," she said.

While profit for both council and state have certainly been a driver of the partnership, Blakeley thinks that forging greater links to the community could be something City's owners see "as a beneficial side effect."

State-owned clubs starting to think smart despite concerns

After 18 years in the club and city, the UAE are deeply embedded in this part of Manchester. With political ties between the UK and UAE now reportedly strained as a result of the charges, there are suggestions that City's owners will try to sell the club. They may also be forced to do so, with sanctions still to be decided pending City's appeal.

There is no such trouble at PSG, who look capable of winning a third straight Champions League powered by their own Gulf-State coffers.

What is clear is that state-owned football clubs can become successful fast in a free market, as the Premier League was when the UAE owners arrived. Deep pockets, strong contacts at the top tables of the sport and canny strategies to integrate with the local area can be a heady mix.

It's certainly one that's proved intoxicating to City's fans, who brush off secret second contracts, sham sponsorship and unreliable witnesses with a loyalty built on success, community and investment. Judging by the mood in Manchester on Wednesday, no sanctions are going to change that.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

entries.title: North Korea, China open border bridge after 12-year delay
entries.summary: Twelve years after it was constructed, the New Yalu River Bridge between China and North Korea is finally operational. It is the latest sign of warming ties between the two nations.
entries.content:
China

North Korea, China open border bridge to boost trade

October 15, 2026

Twelve years after it was constructed, the New Yalu River Bridge between China and North Korea is finally operational. It is the latest sign of warming ties between the two nations.

China and North Korea on Thursday officially opened their most significant land border crossing, aimed at rejuvenating trade and commerce after years of strained ties and disruptions.

A ceremony was held to launch the New Yalu River Bridge, Chinese state media Xinhua News reported.

Meanwhile, China News Service showed visuals of trucks adorned with the national flags of China and North Korea on the bridge, which itself was decorated in flags.

Spectators crowded on a road on the Chinese side, in Dandong city, overlooking the ceremony. In Sinuiju city on the North Korean side, work on the approaching road and compound remained unfinished.

'A new chapter'

The cable-stayed bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused until now due to lack of connecting roads on the North Korean side, South Korea's Yonhap News agency reported.

The opening was further delayed by the COVID pandemic which prompted North Korea to close its borders. Train journeys between the East Asian neighbors only restarted in March after six years, but Pyongyang is yet to resume issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, which once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.

The bridge's opening marks the latest sign of warning ties between Beijing and Pyongyang which have conducted two summits between their leaders in the past year.

"(Bilateral) relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter," Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in ​a video address at the opening, the official Xinhua news agency said.

He added that the border crossing would "strongly promote" economic and trade cooperation and strengthen exchanges between their people.

A conduit for trade

Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told the AFP news agency he expected hundreds of vehicles to cross every day.

"The bridge could become a conduit for China's abundant goods and resources to flow into North Korea and give its economy a significant boost," he said.

At the same time, experts believe North Korea remains cautious of greater dependence on China.

"The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return ‌to pre-sanctions ​trade," said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies. But it will help move heavy equipment and raw material North Korea needs for development, he said.

China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner despite a series of UN sanctions banning the flow of goods and workers to North Korea over its missile and nuclear weapons program.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: EU summit to focus on China, Ukraine and bloc budget
entries.summary: EU leaders meeting in Brussels will examine measures to curb the bloc's huge trade deficit with China. But they will also be looking to further agreement on the next EU budget ahead of some major elections next year.
entries.content:
Europe

EU summit to focus on China, Ukraine and bloc budget

October 15, 2026

EU leaders meeting in Brussels will examine measures to curb the bloc's huge trade deficit with China. But they will also be looking to further agreement on the next EU budget ahead of some major elections next year.

European Union leaders are to meet in Brussels on Thursday for two days of talks that will focus on some of the major economic challenges facing the bloc, including competition from China.

The meeting is also likely to see some heated debate over the bloc's budget for the years 2028 to 2034, with the usual divisive negotiations between net contributors and net recipients.

On Friday, leaders are set to discuss further support for Ukraine as it faces a full-scale Russian invasion, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy due to attend.

Here are the main topics on the agenda:

Chinese competition in focus

The leaders are expected to discuss ways to remedy the bloc's massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.

The meeting comes less than a week after the bloc's executive body, the European Commission, reached an agreement with Beijing to curb imports of hybrid cars from China.

The EU has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field.

Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.

Ahead of the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for new EU measures to counter any actions leading to market distortion.

The leaders will, however, also be looking at soaring energy prices within the bloc as another factor weighing on its competitiveness.

Divisive EU budget

The bloc's next seven-year budget from 2028 to 2034 is also set to be another controversial issue on the agenda, ahead of a special summit set for November to try to reach agreement.

Discussions on the budget, which requires unanimous approval, are often intense, with divisions between wealthier states and those that rely on EU cohesion funds.

The talks at the summit are not expected to bring any breakthrough, but leaders are hoping to reach a compromise by the end of the year.

Pressure to finalize the budget is growing ahead of elections next year in several member states that could make it even more difficult to reach a deal acceptable to all.

Ukraine support

The EU leaders are expected to turn their attention to the situation in Ukraine on Friday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy invited to join the meeting.

He is likely to urge the bloc to up its support for Kyiv as Russia intensifies its strikes ahead of winter, killing dozens of civilians.

European aid is taking on ever more importance as the US under President Donald Trump continues its ambivalent path with regard to the conflict, as reflected in a recent deal securing Russian diesel imports despite international sanctions.

Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukrainian leader.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping
entries.summary: New Delhi wants Moscow and Kyiv to ensure safe commercial shipping in the Black Sea amid attacks that put Indian seafarers at risk.
entries.content:
Ukraine

India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping

October 15, 2026

New Delhi wants Moscow and Kyiv to ensure safe commercial shipping in the Black Sea amid attacks that put Indian seafarers at risk.

India has urged both Russia and Ukraine to ensure safe passage for commercial shipping through the Black Sea as attacks on merchant vessels put Indian seafarers at risk and threaten to disrupt vital food and energy supplies. 

New Delhi says discussions with both sides are under way.

"The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways must be restored at the earliest," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said last week.

India accounts for more than 12% of the global seafaring workforce, with 311,936 maritime professionals, according to a 2026 industry report. And attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Black Sea in recent months have highlighted the risks facing civilian crews.

The Turkish-owned MV Royad Mammadov, a cargo ship carrying grain from Ukraine, caught fire and sank following an attack on Monday, killing two crew members. The three Indian nationals aboard the vessel survived, but sustained injuries and were taken to Romania to receive medical treatment.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for launching the strike.

The Defense Ministry in Moscow separately said it had struck two Ukrainian cargo vessels in the Black Sea but did not specifically identify the ships.

The Liberian-flagged oil tanker Aframax Rio was also recently attacked by unmanned vessels off Russia's Black Sea coast near Sochi, according to Russian authorities. The vessel was carrying 23 Indians, but all of them were rescued.

Can diplomacy deliver safety?

Anil Wadhwa, a former Indian diplomat, said India's proposal to halt attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea covered energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain and energy exports, and an end to strikes on merchant vessels.

"Securing an ironclad guarantee depends entirely on a broader cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine in the maritime theater," Wadhwa told DW.

India's close relations with Russia and expanding engagement with Ukraine give New Delhi access to both sides, but do not guarantee either will honor a shipping arrangement.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has described India's proposal for a possible ceasefire with Russia as the "broadest" of the four offers Kyiv has received.

Russia has not publicly endorsed a binding safe-passage deal proposed by India, despite welcoming New Delhi's peace efforts.

Rajan Kumar of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University said India could use its diplomatic leverage with Moscow to help bring the two sides towards an agreement.

"India could play a constructive role in facilitating dialogue between Russia and Ukraine, particularly on the issue of ensuring the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea," Kumar told DW.

Working with other powers to reach a deal

He argued that India should also work with other influential countries from the Global South, particularly China, Brazil and South Africa.

"A coordinated approach with these countries could enhance their collective diplomatic leverage and strengthen their capacity to persuade both parties to adopt mutually acceptable arrangements for maritime security," said Kumar.

India's initiative comes as US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend, although its scope and implementation mechanism remain unclear.

Harsh Pant, vice president of the New Delhi-based think tank Observer Research Foundation, said Trump's intervention could help India's efforts but might produce a narrower agreement that fails to address New Delhi's wider concerns.

"The energy ceasefire could be an initial confidence-building measure, whereas a Black Sea shipping arrangement requires additional commitments on attacks against merchant vessels, ports, maritime routes and the security of commercial traffic," Pant told DW.

"India need not compete with Washington for the public credit of mediation. It could instead press for the inclusion of broader maritime provisions in any US agreement.”

Will India face a higher import bill?

Wadhwa said the proposed energy truce could also benefit Indian seafarers if it secured safe passage for energy cargoes.

"Although Ukraine alleges that the Russians have already breached this so-called truce, there will be pressure on both sides to allow energy cargoes safe passage. India is bound to gain as far as its crews are concerned in such a scenario," he said.

The disruption to Black Sea shipping also has other implications for India such as delays in shipments of key commodities and higher transport costs.

"A prolonged Black Sea disruption would elevate India's import bill mainly via higher freight on Russian crude and constrained soft oil supplies, with the strongest near-term transmission to domestic edible oil prices and food inflation," said Lekha Chakraborty, professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru
